name: Tomas Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sounds good. I've never done one of these, so stop me if I ramble.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior at Kerr Contracting, about twelve of us, and we do fit-outs: shops, cafés, offices on the business park outside town. Most days I'm on a stepladder running containment and pulling cable, then Paul, my supervisor, does the terminations and I watch and ask questions. I like the team and the banter at break in the van. What wears me down is the early start, the 40-minute drive, and knowing I'm still on the lowest rate on the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So basically nothing. A few emails get written by a bot and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the hype was overblown, let's talk about wages instead. At the pub I'd say the real problem was never robots, it was pay for juniors. Online I'd probably share something from the union about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm still stuck, because nothing changing means I'm still on junior rate with about 400 in the bank. Kerr is steady, so I don't think I'm losing my job, but there are only three electrical firms in town. A steady wage in a town with three electrical firms isn't a career. It's a waiting room with good lighting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Kerr and ask Paul to sign me off on more tasks so I can move up a pay band. I'd put 25 a week into a savings pot with Ines, my girlfriend, so we're not scraping by every month. I'd keep using the chatbot on my phone now and then to check cable sizes before I ask Paul.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. My job's fine, it's just that fine isn't enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you check cable sizes with a chatbot. Do you trust it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half trust it. I use it to check I'm in the right ballpark, then I always ask Paul or look in the regs book. Once it gave me an answer that would have cooked a cable, so I never take its word alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ines say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines would say good, because she teaches at a nursery and nobody's replacing her with a robot either. She'd say the problem is we both earn too little to save. She's right, and she'd tell me to stop moaning and ask for that pay band.

say: I'd say the hype was overblown and **junior wages** are the real problem.
I'd share the **union's** posts about pay for apprentices and juniors.
think: Kerr Contracting is **steady**, so my job feels safe.
On **junior rate** with about 400 saved and three local firms, I feel stuck.
do: Ask Paul to **sign me off** on more tasks to reach the next pay band.
Put **25 a week** into a shared savings pot with Ines.
Keep checking cable sizes with a **chatbot**, then confirm with Paul.
feel: Uneasy rather than scared, because **fine isn't enough**.
S0.quote: A steady wage in a town with three electrical firms isn't a career. It's a waiting room with good lighting.
fieldNote: His job feels **secure**, but low pay and few local firms leave him stuck.
He uses AI **carefully**, always double-checking against his supervisor or the regs.
His girlfriend's view keeps him focused on **pay**, not technology.

steps.text: Ask Paul for sign-off on terminations to reach the next pay band
Put 25 a week into the shared pot with Ines
Use the chatbot to check cable sizes before asking Paul

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first. I can see that hitting the office side of our work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains from AI should go to workers, not just bosses, and I'd say that at the union branch. I'd say we need retraining money for the office staff who get hit first. With friends I'd be calmer, more like, it's coming, let's be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried in a roundabout way. About 40 percent of Kerr's work is office fit-outs on the business park. Every office that needs half the desks needs half the sockets. Fewer office workers means fewer jobs for the lads who wire their offices. If firms shrink their offices, Kerr shrinks, and I'm the cheapest one to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Paul to teach me the quoting software Kerr is bound to bring in, so I'm useful on the planning side as well. I'd go to the union's meetings about AI and push for a rule that juniors finish their training. I'd keep the 25 a week going and stop buying lunch from the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. My hands are safe, but my firm's customers aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me and Kayleigh, the other junior, because we're last in. And Sandra in Kerr's office, because she does the quotes and the ordering, which is exactly what this card says goes first. Sandra's been there 20 years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the quoting software. Isn't that helping the thing that hurts you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yeah. But if Kerr brings it in anyway, I'd rather be the junior who can use it than the one who can't. I'd still fight at the union for it to be fair.

say: I'd say **AI gains** should go to workers, not just bosses.
I'd call for **retraining money** for office staff who get hit first.
think: About **40 percent** of Kerr's work is office fit-outs on the business park.
Fewer office workers means fewer fit-outs, and as a junior I'm the **cheapest to lose**.
do: Ask Paul to teach me the **quoting software** Kerr will bring in.
Push at the union for a rule that **juniors finish training**.
Keep saving **25 a week** and stop buying lunch from the van.
feel: Anxious, because my **hands are safe** but my firm's customers aren't.
S1.quote: Every office that needs half the desks needs half the sockets. Fewer office workers means fewer jobs for the lads who wire their offices.
fieldNote: He traces the risk through his **firm's customers**, not his own tasks.
He worries about Sandra, the **office worker** whose quoting goes first.
He sees the **contradiction** of learning the software that may hurt him and accepts it.

steps.text: Learn Kerr's new AI quoting software from Paul
Push the union for a rule that juniors finish training
Keep saving 25 a week and bring lunch from home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. That's barely after I'd finish my next qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster that governments saw coming and didn't stop. I'd be out with the union calling for income support and a pause on robots in construction. Online I'd be angry, which isn't usually me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the office side of Kerr dies in 2028, and then in 2031 the robots come for the stepladder work. The robots come three years after the brains. Three years is enough to panic, but nowhere near enough to save up on junior pay. I'd be 31 with no licence and a girlfriend on a nursery wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start applying for jobs in the public sector, like council housing maintenance, because I think governments would protect those longest. I'd move our savings into paying off the 1,200 left on my van loan. I'd go to every union meeting and march.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I keep thinking about the stepladder. That's the bit I thought was mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car Ines uses goes, and we share my van. The gym goes, the streaming goes. Christmas presents would be small this year, I'd tell my family straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the thinking AI arriving in 2028 that helps you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the theory side, honestly. If an AI can talk me through fault-finding on site, I'd be a better electrician quicker. But better at a job that's ending in 2031 doesn't feel like much.

say: I'd say governments **saw this coming** and didn't stop it.
I'd march with the union for **income support** and a pause on construction robots.
think: Kerr's **office work** dies in 2028, and stepladder work follows with robots in **2031**.
At 31 I'd have **no licence** and a girlfriend on a nursery wage.
do: Apply for **council housing maintenance** jobs that may last longest.
Pay off the **1,200** left on my van loan.
Go to every **union meeting** and march.
feel: Alarmed, because the **stepladder work** I thought was mine has an end date.
S2.quote: The robots come three years after the brains. Three years is enough to panic, but nowhere near enough to save up on junior pay.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** as panic time, not saving time, on his pay.
He looks to the **public sector** as the safest place to wait.
He admits thinking AI could make him **better at the job** just before it ends.

steps.text: Apply for electrical maintenance jobs with the council
Clear the 1,200 left on the van loan
March with the union for income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Robots in 2034. Okay, that gives me a bit of room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years, so let's spend them training people, not just buying robots. I'd push the union to get a retraining fund agreed with the big contractors. With mates I'd say get your licence now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the office side of Kerr still shrinks around 2031. Five years gives me time to get licensed and move into heat pumps and batteries. Robots fitting heat pumps in old houses still feels a long way off. I'm not in a rush, I'd wait until other lads have done the course and see if it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my licence by 2028, then do the heat pump and battery storage course once a couple of people from Kerr have done it first. I'd keep saving 25 a week. I'd get on the union's working group on AI if they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see a path. That's a big difference from two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for others to do the course first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen lads pay for courses that led nowhere, like the smart-home one a few years ago. I'd rather follow someone I trust, like Paul, into something proven. It costs me a few months, maybe, but I can't afford to waste the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ines decide about your future in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still try to rent somewhere with a garden next year, because five years is enough to keep living. But we'd put off a mortgage until I can see whether heat pump work holds up. Ines would want kids in about four years, and I'd want to know I've got work.

say: I'd say five years should go on **training people**, not just buying robots.
I'd push the union for a **retraining fund** with big contractors.
think: Kerr's office work **shrinks around 2031**, but robots in old houses feel far off.
Five years lets me move into **heat pumps** and batteries.
do: Take the **heat pump** and battery course once others at Kerr prove it pays.
Keep saving **25 a week** and join the union's AI working group.
feel: Anxious, but with a **path** in view, unlike the two-year picture.
S3.quote: Five years gives me time to get licensed and move into heat pumps and batteries. Robots fitting heat pumps in old houses still feels a long way off.
fieldNote: Five years turns his alarm into a **plan**, but a cautious one.
He waits for **proof** from trusted colleagues before paying for training.
He and Ines **delay a mortgage**, not their whole life.

steps.text: Take the heat pump and battery storage course after Paul does
Put off a mortgage until heat pump work proves steady

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37 when it hits. 40 when the robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and I'd be pushing for a proper national plan. The union should be at the table now, not in 2035. With friends I'd say it's far off, so let's not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine for a long time. Ten years is long enough to become the electrician who fixes the robots, if someone pays for the training. I'd rather maintain robots than compete with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my licence, then the heat pump course, then look for a course in maintaining automated equipment once it exists and people say it's good. I'd keep up the savings, and once I'm licensed I'd push it to 50 a week. I'd vote for whoever promises to pay for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My work is safe for a long while, but I'd always know the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'if someone pays for the training'. Who should?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firms making the robots and the firms saving money from them. Not me out of a junior wage. That's my politics, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future kids about the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my future kids to learn the thinking and the hands-on side together. The electricians who'll last are the ones who can do both.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** if there's a national plan.
I'd tell friends it's **far off**, so no need to panic.
think: My hands-on work stays **safe for years**, with robots not until 2039.
I'd rather **maintain robots** than compete with them, if training is paid.
do: Finish the **licence**, then the heat pump course.
Take an **automation maintenance** course once colleagues say it's good.
Raise savings to **50 a week** once licensed.
feel: Uneasy, because work is safe but I'd **always know the date**.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to become the electrician who fixes the robots, if someone pays for the training.
fieldNote: With a decade he pictures himself as the **robot maintainer**.
He insists **robot makers and users** should pay for retraining.
His steady style shows again: he'll move once **others prove** the path.

steps.text: Take an automation maintenance course after colleagues try it
Raise savings to 50 a week once licensed

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time and no money to change. What would help is a retraining wage, paid by the firms making money from the robots. If the bosses get the savings from AI and the workers get the risk, people like me end up paying for somebody else's upgrade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about the office staff. Sandra at Kerr does the quoting and ordering, and everyone forgets the people in the office are part of the trade too.

headlineQuote: If the bosses get the savings from AI and the workers get the risk, people like me end up paying for somebody else's upgrade.
portrait: Tomas is a **27-year-old junior** at Kerr Contracting, doing shop and office fit-outs.
He uses a chatbot **now and then**, always checking its answers with his supervisor.
He sees AI's threat through his firm's **office clients** before it reaches his own hands.
Two years' warning **alarms** him, while five or ten let him plan heat pump work.
He wants **firms that profit** from robots to pay for workers' retraining.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no time or money to change trades.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining wage** paid by the firms profiting from robots.
